analysis.one_liner: Lets businesses treat workers as independent contractors for federal taxes when a written contract says so.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by two Republican senators and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a legal 'safe harbor' under the tax code: if a company and a worker sign a written contract stating the worker is not an employee, and the worker meets certain tests (such as having their own business location or equipment, and risking profit or loss), the IRS could not treat the worker as an employee [S2][S3]. Businesses using contractors would no longer owe employer payroll taxes, withholding, or benefit-related costs for those workers, and the IRS would face a higher bar to reclassify them, with past tax bills generally limited going forward [S2][S3]. It would also repeal a 1986 rule that limits the tax code's existing safe harbor for technical-services workers like computer consultants [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that use contract labor — staffing and consulting firms, construction and trucking businesses, and others — would gain certainty against IRS reclassification and avoid employer payroll taxes, benefits obligations, and unemployment insurance contributions for workers who sign the contract. Self-employed contractors and their clients would get clearer tax rules. The repeal of the 1986 technical-services provision would particularly benefit firms placing consultants with clients [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a statutory safe harbor: a worker meeting the tests who signs a written contract declaring non-employee status is not treated as an employee for federal tax purposes, so the client owes no employer payroll taxes or withholding on that work [S2][S3].
Shifts the burden of proof in disputes to the Treasury Secretary once the company makes a basic showing, making it harder for the IRS to reclassify workers as employees [S3].

Limits IRS reclassification of workers to prospective effect from a notice date when the company had a written contract, filed required information returns, and had a reasonable basis, sparing businesses retroactive payroll-tax bills [S2][S3].

Repeals Section 530(d) of the Revenue Act of 1978, the 1986 provision that narrowed the existing safe harbor for technical-services workers, restoring broader relief for staffing and consulting arrangements [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers shifted from employee to contractor status would bear the full self-employment tax (both the employee and employer halves of Social Security and Medicare), lose employer-provided benefits and unemployment insurance coverage, and gain no employer withholding. The Treasury would lose payroll tax revenue. Misclassified workers would also have a harder time challenging their status because the burden of proof would fall on the government [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Contract workers and federal payroll tax revenue

drawbacks.text: The key trigger is a written contract stating the worker is not an employee, which lets a company change a worker's tax status largely by paperwork rather than by the realities of the working relationship — the very factor the common-law test weighs [S3].

Workers reclassified under the safe harbor would pay the full self-employment tax instead of only the employee half, and would lose employer-provided benefits and unemployment insurance coverage, with no requirement that the employer make them whole [S3].

Making IRS reclassifications effective only prospectively, when conditions are met, would erase the government's ability to collect back payroll taxes in many disputes, reducing enforcement against large-scale misclassification [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real value to genuinely independent contractors and their clients, who today face uncertain and inconsistent IRS tests. But because non-employee status can be established largely through a written contract, the bill also opens a broad path for companies to convert employees into contractors, shifting payroll taxes, benefits, and unemployment insurance costs onto the workers themselves and reducing federal revenue. The enforcement limits — burden of proof on the government and prospective-only reclassifications — compound that shift. On balance the costs to workers and the Treasury outweigh the certainty the bill provides.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Bond introduced the bill on March 19, 1997, joined by Sen. Don Nickles as the bill's only cosponsor [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: contract workers kept existing employee-classification rules and Treasury kept its enforcement tools, while businesses seeking easier contractor classification did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo — workers and Treasury unaffected

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — and it died at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's only support on record came from two Republican senators, and it died in a committee chaired by a Republican without recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Temporary staffing, consulting, and contract-labor firms
industries.note: The safe harbor, prospective-only IRS reclassification, and repeal of the 1986 technical-services restriction would let these firms classify workers as contractors, avoiding employer payroll taxes, benefits, and unemployment insurance costs — costs that shift to the workers and the Treasury [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Businesses that use freelance or contract labor broadly (construction, trucking, delivery, professional services)
industries.note: A written contract plus business-like indicators would shield them from IRS reclassification and retroactive payroll-tax liability, giving certainty while shifting tax and benefit costs onto workers [S3].

Genuine contractors and their clients would get clearer, safer tax rules and a home-office test that favors contractor status [S3]. The same rules, however, could be used to convert employees into contractors who bear full self-employment taxes.
